reference.source: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology / Baran and Dawber's Diseases of the Nails
clinicalPearls: A digital myxoid cyst is a benign, dome-shaped, translucent swelling overlying the distal interphalangeal joint or the proximal nail fold of a finger
It is strongly associated with osteoarthritis of the underlying distal interphalangeal joint and is commonest in middle-aged and older adults
Pressure from the cyst on the nail matrix commonly produces a longitudinal groove or gutter in the nail, which can mimic other nail dystrophies
It may discharge a clear, viscous, gelatinous fluid when punctured, reflecting its mucinous content
Many lesions communicate with the joint space through a pedicle, which is relevant to recurrence after treatment
It can be mistaken for a nail tumour, and transillumination and imaging help confirm its cystic nature
Management options range from conservative observation and simple drainage to more definitive treatments addressing the joint connection, such as excision, with recurrence being a recognised problem
reference.pathophysiology: A digital myxoid cyst is a mucin-filled swelling that develops near the distal interphalangeal joint, typically in the setting of underlying osteoarthritis. It is thought to arise either from local overproduction of mucin by fibroblasts in the dermis or from herniation of degenerate joint fluid through a capsular defect, often with a persistent connecting pedicle to the joint. When the cyst lies over the proximal nail fold it presses on the matrix beneath, disturbing plate production and creating a longitudinal groove in the nail; the frequent communication with the joint explains why lesions recur if the connection is not dealt with and why they may intermittently discharge gelatinous fluid.
additionalDifferentials: Giant cell tumour of the tendon sheath
Rheumatoid or gouty nodule over the joint
Subungual or periungual tumour causing a nail groove
additionalInvestigations: Clinical inspection and transillumination of the translucent swelling
Onychoscopy to relate the cyst to any longitudinal nail groove
Radiograph of the digit to demonstrate underlying osteoarthritic changes and osteophytes
Ultrasound or magnetic resonance imaging to confirm the cystic nature and any joint connection
Observation of gelatinous fluid discharge on puncture where appropriate
Histology of an excised specimen if the diagnosis is uncertain
redFlags: Rapid growth, ulceration, or atypical features suggesting a solid tumour rather than a cyst
Signs of septic arthritis or joint infection given the frequent joint communication
Recurrent cysts after treatment indicating an unaddressed joint connection
Persistent nail dystrophy that could reflect an alternative underlying lesion
reference.prognosis: Digital myxoid cysts are benign, and the associated nail groove usually resolves once the cyst is successfully treated and matrix pressure is relieved, but recurrence is common, especially when the connection to the osteoarthritic joint is not addressed.
pitfalls: Mistaking the cyst for a nail tumour and pursuing unnecessary aggressive investigation
Treating the nail groove without recognising and addressing the overlying cyst
Simple drainage alone, which frequently leads to recurrence via the joint pedicle
Overlooking the risk of introducing infection into the joint during intervention
references: Baran and Dawber's Diseases of the Nails and their Management
management: Reassurance regarding the benign nature, with the expectation that relieving matrix pressure resolves the associated nail groove
Conservative measures for recurrent lesions, including repeated aseptic needle puncture and expression, cryotherapy, intralesional corticosteroid or sclerotherapy
Definitive surgical excision with ligation of the joint pedicle and removal of the underlying osteophyte to minimise recurrence
Consider carbon dioxide laser ablation as an alternative destructive option
Management of the underlying distal interphalangeal joint osteoarthritis
Avoid repeated self-drainage because of the risk of introducing infection and septic arthritis through the joint communication
Referral to dermatology or hand surgery for recurrent lesions or when the diagnosis is uncertain
